opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about it along a few dimensions.

The first is whether the field has a good "data engine." AI is only as good as what it learns from, so I look for areas where you either already have large, high-quality datasets, like protein structures in the PDB, or where you can generate data cheaply and reliably, through simulation or high-throughput experiments. If every data point costs a PhD student six months, it's very hard for AI to make a dent.

The second is whether there's a clear, verifiable objective. AlphaFold worked so well partly because protein structure prediction had a well-defined target and a benchmark, CASP, that everyone agreed on. When you can score a prediction against ground truth, you can iterate fast. Fields where success is fuzzy or takes years to validate are harder.

Third, I look at how big the gap is between what the physics allows and what we can currently compute. Many fields have equations we basically know, quantum chemistry, fluid dynamics, materials, but solving them exactly is prohibitively expensive. That's a sweet spot. AI can act as a fast surrogate, learning to approximate expensive simulations at a fraction of the cost, sometimes thousands of times faster.

Fourth is the closed loop with experiments. The most exciting areas are ones where a model's prediction can quickly be tested in a lab, ideally an automated one, and the result fed back into the model. Drug discovery, materials synthesis, and parts of biology are moving that way. Once you close that loop, progress compounds.

And finally there's the value question: if you solve it, does it matter? Better batteries, new drugs, catalysts for clean energy, more efficient chips. These have huge economic and societal payoffs, which also means capital and talent will flow in and sustain the effort.

So if I put it together, life sciences, especially protein and molecular design, and materials science stand out right now. They have the data, the physics, the verifiability, and the payoff all lining up. Areas like climate and weather modeling are also very promising. Others, like a lot of clinical medicine, are important but still bottlenecked by data access and slow validation cycles, so I think they'll take longer.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about which fields are ripe for AI for Science, I mostly look at three things.

The first is whether the field has, or can generate, a lot of high-quality data. AI methods are fundamentally data-hungry, so areas like protein structure, where you had decades of curated crystallography data in the PDB, were almost waiting for something like AlphaFold to happen. Materials science is getting there too, with large computed databases and increasingly automated experiments.

The second is whether the underlying problem has some structure that a model can actually learn, but that's too expensive or too complex to compute from first principles. Quantum many-body systems, molecular dynamics, fluid simulations, these are all cases where we know the equations but can't afford to solve them at the scale we care about. That gap between "we know the physics" and "we can't compute it" is exactly where learned surrogates shine.

The third, and this is the one people underestimate, is whether there's a fast feedback loop for validation. If an AI model proposes a new molecule or a new material, can you test it in days or weeks rather than years? Chemistry and biology are getting much better at this through automation and self-driving labs. Fields where verification is slow or ambiguous are much harder, no matter how good the model is.

Coming from condensed matter physics myself, I'd say my own field is attractive but tricky. We have rich physics and real computational bottlenecks, but experimental data is often sparse and sample-specific. So the near-term wins are probably in things like accelerating simulations and helping with experimental design, rather than AI discovering a new phase of matter on its own. Though I wouldn't rule that out in the longer run.

astra-6.text:
I’d look at three things. First, is there an important scientific problem where progress is limited by something AI could help with—for example, searching a very large space of possible molecules or analyzing measurements that are difficult to interpret?

Second, is there a way for the model to learn? That might mean high-quality experimental data, or simulations that can generate useful training examples. The key is whether that information captures the phenomenon you actually care about.

Third, can you test the result? A model can produce a very convincing prediction, but in science you need a way to establish whether it’s correct. Fields where you can move quickly from prediction to experiment and feed the results back into the model are particularly attractive.

So I’d judge specific problems more than entire disciplines. Within the same field, one problem might have abundant data and a clear experimental test, while another has very little data and takes years to validate. The most promising opportunities combine scientific importance with a practical way to learn and verify.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d look at three things. First, is there an important scientific problem where the existing approach has hit a bottleneck? Second, can AI actually learn something useful from the available data? And third, can we test its predictions and use the results to improve the model?

That third point is particularly important. A model can generate a very convincing hypothesis, but science requires verification. If experiments are relatively fast and affordable, you can build a cycle of prediction, experiment, and feedback. If every experiment takes several years, progress will be much harder.

So I wouldn’t judge a field simply by how much data it has or how fashionable it is. I’d look for a specific problem where better predictions change what scientists can do, and where there’s a practical path to checking whether those predictions are right.
